drills.q: Why does a model predicting 'O' for every token still score high token-level accuracy?
drills.a: Real NER corpora are dominated by O (outside-entity) tokens, often 80-95%+, so predicting O everywhere matches the majority class most of the time while extracting zero actual entities.

drills.q: What's the difference between the forward algorithm and Viterbi decoding in a CRF?
drills.a: The forward algorithm (with backward, for training) sums over ALL possible tag sequences to compute Z(x) and expected feature counts for the gradient. Viterbi uses max instead of sum to find the single best-scoring legal sequence for prediction. Same DP structure, different operation and purpose.

drills.q: Derive why naive computation of a CRF's partition function is exponential and how forward-backward fixes it.
drills.a: Z(x) = Σ over every possible tag sequence y', T^n of them for T tags and n tokens -- exponential. The score decomposes into a sum of local terms depending only on adjacent tag pairs, so the forward algorithm computes it via DP in O(n*T^2): the forward variable at position t aggregates all paths ending at each tag from position t-1's forward variables.

drills.q: A transformer NER model performs well on aggregate metrics but produces inconsistent boundaries specifically on multi-word brand names. What's the likely bug and how do you catch it before shipping?
drills.a: Likely a subword-to-word label alignment bug: labels applied inconsistently across a word's subword pieces (e.g. full B-TYPE label copied onto every subword instead of only the first, with remainder masked/relabeled). Catch it with a unit test using a known multi-subword entity that round-trips through tokenize -> align labels -> train step -> decode -> reassemble to word-level spans.

drills.q: Design an active learning loop for a new entity type your model performs poorly on.
drills.a: Score the unlabeled pool with the current model, rank by uncertainty (margin between top-1/top-2 Viterbi sequence scores, or aggregated token entropy for softmax models), send highest-uncertainty sentences to annotators, retrain, repeat. Combine with diversity sampling (cluster sentence embeddings) to avoid repeatedly selecting near-duplicate hard examples. Stop when marginal F1 gain per labeled batch drops below a cost-justified threshold.

drills.q: Why might a hybrid rule-plus-model approach beat a pure NER model for entities like PRICE or FLIGHT_NUMBER?
drills.a: These have highly regular surface forms (currency symbols/digit patterns, airline-code-plus-digits) that a regex handles with near-perfect precision at zero training cost. Reserve the trained model's capacity for linguistically variable entity types (hotel names, amenities) that rules genuinely can't capture.

drills.q: How do you handle nested entities like a city name inside a full airport name, given standard BIO tagging can't represent them?
drills.a: Options: redesign the schema to avoid the nesting if the inner entity isn't independently needed, run a layered extraction pass (extract outer span, then re-run a focused extractor on its text for the inner entity), or adopt a nested-NER-specific architecture (span-based/hypergraph) only if nesting is frequent and both entities are independently needed downstream.

drills.q: Compare fine-tuned transformer NER against zero-shot LLM extraction for a high-volume production content pipeline, and describe a hybrid that captures both advantages.
drills.a: Fine-tuned NER wins at high volume/low latency/cost per document (thousands of docs/sec feasible). Zero-shot LLM wins for new or rapidly-changing low-volume schemas where fine-tuning cost isn't justified. Hybrid: use LLM extraction to weakly label a large unlabeled corpus quickly, human-review a sample (active-learning-prioritized), and train a cheaper fine-tuned model on that data to serve production traffic.

drills.q: Design the end-to-end entity extraction pipeline for a hotel-listing corpus needing DESTINATION, ROOM_TYPE, PRICE, and AMENITY tags at millions-of-documents scale.
drills.a: Split by regularity: PRICE via regex (near-perfect precision, negligible cost). DESTINATION/ROOM_TYPE via a fine-tuned BiLSTM-CRF or lightweight transformer, evaluated with entity-level F1 via seqeval, cheap enough for full corpus scale. AMENITY (open-ended, growing) via active learning with periodic retraining as new phrasings appear. Bootstrap model training data via LLM weak-labeling plus human review rather than fully manual annotation. A single architecture for the whole schema is the wrong call.

drills.q: Why does global normalization in a CRF fix the label bias problem that plagues MEMMs?
drills.a: MEMMs normalize transition probabilities locally at each step, which structurally biases the model toward states with fewer outgoing transitions regardless of the actual observation. A CRF normalizes once, globally, over the whole tag sequence via the partition function Z(x), so no state is penalized purely for having a smaller local branching factor.
